extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, copy editors, and readers interested in news writing and journalistic style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria about the linguistic register 'journalese' used in news media, what makes it problematic, when it can be useful, and editorial practices to address it. Useful for writers, editors, and style-watchers evaluating or producing news copy and headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid artificial/hyperbolic/over-abbreviated language (journalese)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalese is the artificial or hyperbolic, and sometimes over-abbreviated, language regarded as characteristic of the news style used in popular media.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joe Grimm likened journalese to a 'stage voice': it is written out of habit or misguided training to sound urgent or authoritative but often fails to do so. Examples include turns of phrase such as 'hammered out agreement' or 'called for tighter restrictions'. Journalese can dress up something as more significant or interesting and may indicate a flimsy story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichéd or familiar phrases under time pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists, who write many similar stories under time pressure, may fall back on clichéd or familiar phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics note that such reliance on formulaic phrasing produces stilted language. Being aware of this tendency helps writers avoid lazy repetition and cliché.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overuse terms with specific legal meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms with legal meanings, such as 'mayhem', may be overused to the point that they become meaningless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gratuitous use of legally loaded words; repeated or loose usage dilutes meaning and can mislead readers about legal significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rare, archaic, or 'fossil' words used as journalese
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalese often appears as specific word choice: rare or archaic words such as 'ink' (as a verb), 'nab', 'slated', 'ailing', 'quizzed' (in place of 'asked' or 'questioned'), 'funnyman', or synonyms of 'attack' to mean 'criticise'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such fossil words can persist in idiomatic journalese statements. Sometimes they are chosen to save space by using shorter words or phrases, but writers should prefer clarity over quaint or showy word choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use brevity appropriately—headlinese influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Brevity is particularly important in headlines, which have their own idiosyncratic style called headlinese; headlinese's focus on using the smallest possible words has influenced the vocabulary choice of news stories themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious that the need for short words in headlines can bleed into story copy; balance concision with clarity and natural phrasing to avoid awkward or misleading constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anthropomorphization constructions (e.g., 'saw' constructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anthropomorphization is another form of journalese, such as with the use of the verb 'saw' in the phrase 'The 1990s saw an increase in crime' to avoid 'Crime increased in the 1990s'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constructions are often used to avoid straightforward active formulations and can be a marker of journalese; prefer direct, active phrasing where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize onomatopoeia, awkward genitives, and gap-filler constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Other forms include use of onomatopoeia, genitives of place names ('New York's Central Park' rather than 'Central Park, in New York'), and gap filler articles like 'bus plunge' stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such devices can make copy colorful but may also reflect lazy or formulaic reporting; editors should evaluate whether they aid comprehension or merely add sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid passive voice and 'weasel wording' that hides actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics fault the use of the passive voice and similar constructions in journalese as a form of weasel wording where the writer chooses 'to hide the culprit' of the action being described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passive constructions can mask responsibility and are often read as signs of weak evidence or evasiveness. Prefer active voice to make agency clear unless passive is necessary for factual or legal reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial removal and flagging of egregious journalese
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspaper subeditors (copy editors) are often trained to remove journalese, and The New York Times has a customised grammar checker that flags egregious journalese examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial processes should include training and tools to detect and remove journalese; use copy-editing and automated checks to enforce clearer, more precise writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize when simplified journalese improves comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Some people regard journalese with amusement, and some terms can make news reports easier to understand, such as replacing complex jargon with simple and concise phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the general rule against journalese with the pragmatic benefit of replacing dense jargon with accessible language. Use plain-language substitutions when they genuinely aid reader understanding without resorting to clichés or misleading phrasing.
